newsitem.title: BRAZIL: OLYMPICS-RIO TRY TO PROJECT SERIOUS IMAGE IN 2004 BID.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-RIO TRY TO PROJECT SERIOUS IMAGE IN 2004 BID.

text.p: Organisers of Rio de Janeiro's Olympic bid know only too well that the delights of the "Cidade Maravilhosa" are not enough on their own to win the right to host the 2004 Games.
The Rio 2004 committee has made a huge effort to regain the credibility lost by the capital Brasilia's bungled bid for the 2000 Olympics.

Brasilia, whose bid lacked the support of the government, the public and even the country's National Olympic committee, bowed to pressure from the International Olympic Committee and eventually withdrew its candidature before the final vote.

Renowned as a fun-loving city -- although many visitors express disappoint with the lack of variety in the nightlife -- Rio has tried to project the image of competence and good organisation as much as sea and samba.

The Rio committee believes that its bid is technically as good as any other and has placed the emphasis of its campaign on this. And it prefers to leave the seductive charm of the city as something that could swing the balance in its favour rather than the mainstay of the argument.
"I see Rio as the favourite," said Ronaldo Cesar Coelho, president of the Rio 2004 committee last week.

A huge publicity campaign has mobilised public opinion and a recent poll showed 84 percent of the population to be in favour of staging the Games. President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and sporting celebrities such as Pele have given their backing.
Rio's massive social problems, with large segments of the population living in notorious shanty-towns known as favelas, are an obvious stumbling block.
But Coelho insists that, by attracting investments in infrastructure which would otherwise not be forthcoming, the Olympic Games will help solve these problems rather than exacerbate them.
"We've made no secret of our shortcomings. We actually took the IOC members into a favela. How many other candidate cities could have done that," he said.

Rio plans to stage all the main events in the city itself, with both the purpose-built Olympic stadium and village to be built within walking distance of each other an island that houses the city's dilapidated federal university.

Other venues would be concentrated into five areas, all on main highways which organisers believe would spare visitors being trapped in the city's infernal traffic. The famous Maracana stadium would be used just for the soccer event.
An estimated $1.7 billion in investments would be needed, of which $1 billion would come from the private sector.
Rio's biggest problem is convincing the IOC that visitors will not be mugged during their stay.

In fact, most foreign visitors to the city encounter few problems and nearly all say that its reputation is grossly exaggerated. Even when muggings occur, robbers rarely harm their victims and many will return credit cards and leave enough money to catch a bus home if requested.
Most of Rio's murder victims are claimed by the drugs war or domestic arguments which, in a country where gun ownership is high, turn to shootouts.

Coelho points to the 1992 Earth Summit as proof that visitors have nothing to fear. "In 1992 we had 114 heads of state here and there was no trouble. On New Year's Eve, two million people went to the beach and there was no incident," he said. "We have everything you need to stage the best Games of the modern era."
But if visitors do not need to clutch their wallets, they may wish to hold onto their noses.
Pollution is one of the city's big drawbacks. Enough sewage to fill the Maracana is pours into the Guanabara Bay, on which the city stands, every day.
The water which surrounds the proposed Olympic venue exudes an appalling stench which obliges passing motorists to wind up their windows.
Authorities have pledged a massive clean up by 2004 but similar promises in the past, made in conjunction with the staging of the Earth Summit, have not been fulfilled because of political wrangling.
